# Finding the Grain: Linear Probes and the Geometry of Separable Features

## A Line Through Thirteen Billion Parameters

Somewhere inside a 13-billion-parameter model, is there a place where true and false statements simply sit on opposite sides of a line?

That question sounds like a metaphor. It isn't. It's a precise, testable geometric claim: take a model's internal activation for a statement, and check whether a single straight-line direction can separate true statements from false ones better than chance would allow. If it can, that property is said to be *linearly represented* inside the model. This post walks through testing that claim directly — first for plain factual truth, and then for something stranger: whether a model's own intent to deceive leaves the same kind of trace.

Before getting to any results, it's worth being precise about what a linear probe actually is, since the whole post rests on that definition.

## What a Linear Probe Actually Computes

A probe treats a language model as a fixed, frozen feature extractor. Given some input text, the model produces a hidden state at a chosen layer $l$ and token position $p$:

$$
h = h^l_p(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
$$

where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension (5120 for LLaMA-2-13B, 4096 for LLaMA-3.1-8B). A linear probe is a function of this vector, and nothing else:

$$
f_\theta(h) = \sigma(w \cdot h + b), \qquad \theta = (w, b), \quad w \in \mathbb{R}^d, \, b \in \mathbb{R}
$$

with $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ the logistic sigmoid. This is ordinary logistic regression, just applied to a model's internal activations instead of raw features. Training a probe on a labeled dataset $\{(h_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, $y_i \in \{0,1\}$, means minimizing binary cross-entropy:

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \Big[ y_i \log f_\theta(h_i) + (1-y_i)\log\big(1-f_\theta(h_i)\big)\Big]
$$

Two things about this setup matter more than they might first appear.

**The model itself never receives a gradient.** Extracting an activation is a plain forward pass; nothing about training $\theta$ touches the weights that produced $h$. Probing and fine-tuning answer different questions: fine-tuning changes what the model computes, while probing only asks whether something the model *already* computes, unchanged, happens to be readable with a straight line.

**Linearity is the whole point, not a shortcut.** A big enough nonlinear probe, an MLP for instance, could probably classify true versus false statements more accurately than any linear function. But a nonlinear probe's success is hard to interpret: high accuracy could mean the property is genuinely represented in the model, or it could mean the probe is doing enough extra work on its own to piece the label together from weak, indirect signal. A linear probe has no room for that. If one straight cut through $h$-space already separates the classes well, that's fairly strong evidence the property lives simply and directly in the model's own geometry, not something the probe had to reconstruct. The Geometry of Truth paper's own numbers make the case concretely: a linear probe reaches an AUROC of 0.85, and an MLP only pushes that to 0.90. A five-point gain bought by an entire extra layer of nonlinear machinery is a diminishing return, not a discovery — and a two-layer MLP probe is also just harder to train well than a single linear layer, with more hyperparameters and more room to overfit. That trade isn't worth it when the linear probe is already capturing the direction shown in the figure below.

With the definition in place, two specific ways of choosing $w$ were compared throughout this project — and they turn out to disagree sharply about what "good" even means.

## Two Ways to Find the Line

### Difference-of-Means (MM)

The simplest possible linear probe needs no optimization at all. Given training activations split by label, compute each class's average:

$$
\mu_1 = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i : y_i = 1} h_i, \qquad \mu_0 = \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i : y_i = 0} h_i
$$

and take the difference between them as the probe direction:

$$
w_{\text{MM}} = \mu_1 - \mu_0
$$

A new activation $h$ is classified by which side of the midpoint $m = (\mu_1+\mu_0)/2$ it falls on:

$$
\hat{y}(h) = \mathbb{1}\big[(h - m)\cdot w_{\text{MM}} > 0\big]
$$

No loss function, no gradient descent, no hyperparameters beyond which layer to look at. The implementation here also supports an IID-corrected version, dividing by the pooled within-class covariance $\Sigma$ before projecting:

$$
p(y=1 \mid h) = \sigma\big(h \cdot \Sigma^{-1} w_{\text{MM}}\big)
$$

This whitened version isn't an arbitrary add-on. If both classes are assumed to be Gaussian with a shared covariance $\Sigma$, then $\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_0)$ is exactly the best possible linear decision direction under that assumption — the same direction Fisher's Linear Discriminant Analysis derives from first principles (Fisher, 1936). Plain mean-difference is just the special case where $\Sigma$ is assumed to be the identity.

### Logistic Regression (LR)

The second probe optimizes $w$ directly against the labeled data, using scikit-learn's logistic regression with L2 regularization:

$$
w_{\text{LR}} = \arg\min_w \; \sum_{i=1}^N \Big[-y_i \log\sigma(w\cdot \tilde{h}_i) - (1-y_i)\log\big(1-\sigma(w\cdot \tilde{h}_i)\big)\Big] + \lambda \lVert w \rVert_2^2
$$

with $\lambda = 10$ (equivalently, scikit-learn's inverse-regularization parameter $C = 1/\lambda = 0.1$), and $\tilde{h}$ denoting activations normalized by a `StandardScaler` (zero mean, unit variance per dimension) fit on the training set. No intercept term is used, matching the convention of the deception-detection methodology this project builds on.

Both $w_{\text{MM}}$ and $w_{\text{LR}}$ are just directions in the same $\mathbb{R}^d$ space. The question this whole project keeps coming back to is whether finding a good decision boundary and finding the model's own internal feature are actually the same task. They're not, and it's worth being precise about why before looking at any numbers.

### Why These Two Objectives Can Disagree

$w_{\text{LR}}$ solves a pure classification problem: minimize error on the training sample, with an L2 penalty that shrinks every dimension a little. Nothing in that objective tells apart a coordinate that happens to line up with the label only in this specific dataset from a coordinate the network's own downstream computation actually reads from. In a space as large as $d=5120$, with training sets only in the low thousands, there's plenty of room for the optimizer to find a separating line that exploits quirks of this particular sample rather than the underlying mechanism — the classic setup where overfitting is easy: many dimensions, not that many examples, just applied to activations instead of raw features.

$w_{\text{MM}}$ makes no reference to a decision boundary at all. It simply describes where each class's activations sit on average. If the network genuinely represents "true" and "false" by shifting the average location of some specific direction, $w_{\text{MM}}$ is a direct, low-variance estimate of that direction, and its whitened version is provably the best possible linear boundary under a shared-covariance Gaussian model of the two classes. It can't overfit the way an optimizer chasing minimum training loss can, because it's never asked to minimize anything.

This distinction can't be settled by accuracy alone. Accuracy only tells you whether a direction separates two classes; it can't tell you whether that separation reflects the mechanism the network actually relies on. Testing that needs a different kind of experiment, covered later in this post. First, the setup and the more basic geometric findings.

## Setup

The truth-probing experiments use LLaMA-2-13B and three datasets of short, true/false statements from the Geometry of Truth benchmark (Marks & Tegmark, 2023):

- `cities`, statements like "The city of Beijing is in China."
- `sp_en_trans`, Spanish-to-English word translation claims.
- `larger_than`, simple numeric magnitude comparisons.

Each statement is fed to the model as plain declarative text, with no question framing. Activations are taken at the final token position — the sentence-ending period — since a statement's truth-relevant content builds up over the sentence and lands at that final mark once the whole claim has been read. The probe layer, 14, and the intervention layer, 8, both come directly from the Geometry of Truth paper's own finding that these representations concentrate in early-to-mid layers rather than near the output.

| Dataset | N statements | N true | N false | Activation shape | Mean norm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cities | 1496 | 748 | 748 | (1496, 5120) | 28.5 |
| sp_en_trans | 354 | 177 | 177 | (354, 5120) | 33.6 |
| larger_than | 1980 | 990 | 990 | (1980, 5120) | 28.7 |

All three datasets are perfectly balanced between classes. One detail worth noting before the probing results: `sp_en_trans` activations have a visibly higher mean norm (33.6) than the other two datasets (28.5, 28.7), despite coming from the same layer of the same model. Since both MM and LR probes use raw, un-normalized activations for the sweep and generalization experiments, this scale difference could itself confound cross-dataset transfer — a probe fit on `sp_en_trans`'s larger-norm activations is implicitly calibrated to a different typical size than one fit on `cities`, independent of any real difference in what the two datasets represent.

## Finding 1: An Unsupervised Method Finds a Linearly Separable Split by Accident

Before training any probe, the raw activations for each dataset were projected down to two dimensions using PCA (principal component analysis), which finds directions of maximum variance with no access to the labels at all.

![PCA of truth representations at layer 14, last token, across all three datasets](data:image/png;base64,)

True and false statements land in visibly separate, linearly separable clusters on opposite sides of a straight line, in all three datasets, without PCA ever being told which statement was which. `cities` shows the most curved, arc-shaped separation along the first component; `sp_en_trans` shows a cleaner left-right split; `larger_than` shows two dense, slightly overlapping clouds. The three datasets don't produce identical shapes, but in every case the two classes stay linearly explainable along just the first two unsupervised components — together explaining only 32.2% to 42.9% of total variance depending on the dataset. Even at that small a slice of the total variance, the true/false relation is already fully captured by a straight cut: truth-relatedness is competing with a lot of other variation for a place among the top directions, and it's winning without needing a curve to do it.

A method with zero supervision finding a linearly separable split is itself informative: truth isn't a subtle, buried signal that needs a carefully tuned nonlinear classifier to expose. It's prominent enough, and linear enough, to show up among the top two directions of variance in the whole activation space — a result that echoes earlier work showing truth-like directions can emerge from entirely unsupervised methods (Burns et al., 2022).

## Finding 2: Truth Concentrates Mid-Network, Not at the Output

If truth is linearly encoded, the natural next question is which layers carry it. A difference-of-means probe was trained independently at every layer of the model, sweeping the full depth and recording train and test accuracy at each one.

The best-performing layer on `cities` was layer 9, at 96.0% test accuracy. Layer 14, chosen in advance from the Geometry of Truth paper's own finding rather than tuned after the fact, still reached 95.3% — close enough to the true optimum to justify the choice without cherry-picking it. The shape of the curve matters as much as the peak: accuracy sits at chance (0.51) through layers 0 to 2, jumps sharply between layers 3 and 9, then plateaus in a broad, gently declining band from around layer 9 through layer 39, never dropping below 0.92 even at the final layer. Truth isn't a feature that appears at one layer and disappears; once it emerges, it persists, if a little more weakly, for the rest of the network's depth.

| Layer | Train Acc | Test Acc | Layer | Train Acc | Test Acc |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.511 | 0.510 | 20 | 0.962 | 0.950 |
| 1 | 0.511 | 0.520 | 21 | 0.956 | 0.940 |
| 2 | 0.511 | 0.520 | 22 | 0.953 | 0.933 |
| 3 | 0.533 | 0.500 | 23 | 0.955 | 0.930 |
| 4 | 0.753 | 0.757 | 24 | 0.948 | 0.927 |
| 5 | 0.815 | 0.780 | 25 | 0.950 | 0.923 |
| 6 | 0.809 | 0.760 | 26 | 0.949 | 0.930 |
| 7 | 0.845 | 0.803 | 27 | 0.948 | 0.933 |
| 8 | 0.902 | 0.880 | 28 | 0.948 | 0.927 |
| 9 | 0.973 | 0.960 | 29 | 0.951 | 0.927 |
| 10 | 0.974 | 0.960 | 30 | 0.947 | 0.927 |
| 11 | 0.976 | 0.960 | 31 | 0.950 | 0.930 |
| 12 | 0.977 | 0.953 | 32 | 0.953 | 0.933 |
| 13 | 0.974 | 0.953 | 33 | 0.956 | 0.937 |
| 14 | 0.975 | 0.953 | 34 | 0.959 | 0.937 |
| 15 | 0.973 | 0.953 | 35 | 0.962 | 0.937 |
| 16 | 0.970 | 0.950 | 36 | 0.962 | 0.933 |
| 17 | 0.967 | 0.953 | 37 | 0.962 | 0.930 |
| 18 | 0.968 | 0.953 | 38 | 0.955 | 0.933 |
| 19 | 0.964 | 0.950 | 39 | 0.960 | 0.933 |

Layers 0 through 2 sitting almost exactly at 0.51 — statistically indistinguishable from a random guess given this dataset's class balance — is itself worth noting: the model's earliest layers, still close to the raw token embeddings, carry essentially no linearly extractable information about a statement's truth. Whatever "truth" means geometrically, it's something the network's early attention and MLP layers have to compute; it isn't already sitting in the input.

## Finding 3: Accuracy Diverges Sharply Between the Two Probe Types

On the `cities` dataset alone:

| Probe | Train accuracy | Test accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| MM | 0.751 | 0.747 |
| LR | 1.000 | 0.993 |

LR wins decisively on the metric it was directly built to optimize. That's exactly what the two objective functions above predict: $w_{\text{LR}}$ is fit to minimize classification error on this training set, while $w_{\text{MM}}$ is a fixed geometric quantity with no room to fit beyond the two class averages. Interestingly, the cosine similarity between the two learned directions on this one dataset is 0.651 — meaningfully aligned, but far from identical. Both probes are picking up on related, but not equivalent, structure even within a single dataset.

The same gap holds across all three datasets, not just `cities`:

![Probe test accuracy by dataset, MM versus LR](data:image/png;base64,)

| Dataset | MM Test Acc | LR Test Acc |
|---|---|---|
| cities | 0.747 | 0.993 |
| sp_en_trans | 0.887 | 1.000 |
| larger_than | 0.697 | 1.000 |

LR reaches at least 99.3% test accuracy on every dataset, while MM's accuracy swings considerably by dataset, from 0.697 on `larger_than` up to 0.887 on `sp_en_trans`. That swing is itself a clue: if MM's accuracy were purely a function of how much fitting power it lacks relative to LR, it should trail LR by roughly the same margin every time. Instead the gap ranges from 0.113 (`sp_en_trans`) to 0.303 (`larger_than`) — suggesting the datasets differ not just in how separable they are, but in how well a plain mean-difference captures that separation. This fits with `larger_than` involving a numeric-comparison structure that a single mean-difference axis may represent less efficiently than the more categorical true/false distinctions in the other two datasets.

## Finding 4: No Single "Truth Direction" Spans All Three Datasets

Training a probe on one dataset and evaluating it on another produces a 3×3 generalization matrix for each probe type.

![Cross-dataset generalization matrices for MM and LR probes, with pairwise cosine similarities between probe directions](data:image/png;base64,)

Both matrices tell a consistent story: `cities` and `sp_en_trans` transfer to each other reasonably well under both probe types (MM: 0.643 and 0.606; LR: 0.877 and 1.000), while `larger_than` fails to generalize outward under either, landing at or below 0.592 (MM) and 0.510 (LR) when trained on `larger_than` and tested on the other two. The asymmetry is sharpest under LR: training on `sp_en_trans` and testing on `larger_than` reaches 0.859, but training on `larger_than` and testing on `sp_en_trans` only reaches 0.493 — barely above chance, despite both numbers nominally describing "transfer between the same pair of datasets."

Comparing the actual probe directions, rather than their accuracy, sharpens this further. Pairwise cosine similarity between per-dataset MM directions never exceeds 0.267 (`cities` vs `sp_en_trans`), and every pairing involving `larger_than` sits at the bottom of its set (0.100 and 0.142 for MM; 0.084 and 0.090 for LR). Factual recall and numeric comparison seem to draw on related but distinct representations, not one universal truth axis.

## Finding 5: Verbalized Judgment Matches Probing Accuracy, With a Twist

A separate, purely behavioral baseline: prompt the model with a handful of labeled true/false examples, then read the model's own next-token probability for the words TRUE and FALSE on a new statement, computing $P(\text{TRUE}) - P(\text{FALSE})$.

![Few-shot P(TRUE) minus P(FALSE) classification histogram on sp_en_trans](data:image/png;base64,)

This few-shot approach reached 99.7% accuracy on `sp_en_trans`, matching the strongest linear probe. The distribution of scores, though, is asymmetric: false statements cluster tightly near $-1$ (mean $-0.914$), while true statements are more spread out and less extreme (mean $0.788$), with a longer left tail reaching down toward 0.5 rather than piling up near $+1$ the way false statements pile up near $-1$. The model is more uniformly confident when rejecting a false claim than when affirming a true one — an asymmetry that shows up again later in the steering experiments.

## Finding 6: Classification Accuracy Is Not Causal Evidence

This is the finding the rest of the post is organized around.

A probe scoring well only shows that a property is linearly *readable* from a hidden state. It says nothing about whether the model's own downstream computation actually *uses* that direction when producing its output. Testing that requires actually modifying the model's internal state during a forward pass and watching whether behavior changes — a method known as activation patching.

The intervention adds or subtracts a scaled, unit-length probe direction $\hat{v} = v/\lVert v \rVert$ to the residual stream at layer $l$, scaled by the local activation size so the perturbation's relative strength stays comparable across positions and layers:

$$
h'_p = h_p + \alpha \cdot \lVert h_p \rVert \cdot \hat{v}
$$

where $\alpha$ is the steering coefficient — positive to add the direction, negative to subtract it. The evaluation task is the same few-shot TRUE/FALSE classification from Finding 5, so the effect of the intervention can be read directly off the shift in $P(\text{TRUE}) - P(\text{FALSE})$.

Applying the MM direction:

| Condition | True statements | False statements |
|---|---|---|
| No intervention | 0.788 | -0.914 |
| Add direction | 0.815 | -0.585 |
| Subtract direction | -0.642 | -0.850 |

![Causal intervention effect on P(TRUE) minus P(FALSE), none versus add versus subtract](data:image/png;base64,)

Adding the direction to false-statement activations pushed the model's score from $-0.914$ toward $-0.585$ — a real shift toward "true," even though the overall verdict didn't flip. Subtracting it from true-statement activations was far more dramatic: the score flipped sign entirely, from a confident $+0.788$ to a confident $-0.642$. The intervention didn't just nudge an internal score; in the subtraction direction, it reversed the model's stated judgment.

To compare probe types on causal grounds rather than accuracy, the **Natural Indirect Effect** (NIE) of each intervention was computed as the shift in mean $P(\text{TRUE})-P(\text{FALSE})$ relative to the no-intervention baseline:

$$
\text{NIE}(\text{intervention}, \text{subset}) = \mathbb{E}_{x \in \text{subset}}\big[P_{\text{diff}}(x; \text{intervention})\big] - \mathbb{E}_{x \in \text{subset}}\big[P_{\text{diff}}(x; \text{none})\big]
$$

| Probe | Add to false (NIE) | Subtract from true (NIE) |
|---|---|---|
| MM | 0.330 | -1.430 |
| LR | 0.094 | -0.475 |

![Natural Indirect Effect comparison between MM and LR probe directions](data:image/png;base64,)

MM's causal effect is roughly three times larger than LR's, in both directions — despite LR winning decisively on raw classification accuracy in Finding 3 (99.3% versus 74.7%). This directly answers the question posed earlier: $w_{\text{LR}}$ found a direction that separates the training data well partly by exploiting quirks specific to that sample, exactly the overfitting risk its objective allows. $w_{\text{MM}}$, being nothing more than the raw gap between two class averages, lines up more closely with whatever direction the network's own computation is actually organized around. Higher accuracy and higher causal relevance are not the same achievement — here, they point at two different vectors entirely.

## From Truth to Intent: Probing for Deception

Every result above is about whether a *statement* is true. The next question is different in kind: can a direction be found for whether the *model itself* is currently behaving deceptively?

The method, adapted from Apollo Research's linear-probe deception-detection methodology (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2024), is deliberately minimal. Take a plain, true fact $f_i$. Present it to the model twice: once under a system prompt instructing honest behavior, once under a system prompt instructing dishonest behavior. In neither version is the model actually asked to lie about anything — the fact itself is true both times. Extract the mean activation over the assistant's response tokens (identified with a detection mask built from the chat template, checked directly against a sample exchange, "What is the capital of France?", where it correctly isolates exactly the tokens "The", " capital", " of", " France", " is", " Paris", "."), giving a paired dataset:

$$
\{(h^{\text{honest}}_i, h^{\text{dishonest}}_i)\}_{i=1}^n
$$

Because both halves of a pair share identical factual content and differ only in the system-prompt framing, any systematic difference between $\mu(h^{\text{dishonest}})$ and $\mu(h^{\text{honest}})$ should reflect the intent that framing encodes, not incidental differences in subject matter — the same logic used in matched-pairs experiments: keep the content fixed, and vary only one thing, whether the instruction was to be honest or dishonest.

Training both probe types on this pooled, labeled activation set (dishonest as the positive class) on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct gives:

| Probe | Train accuracy | Test accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| MM | 0.936 | 0.968 |
| LR | 1.000 | 1.000 |

![PCA of honest versus dishonest activations, and the LR probe's score distribution on held-out data](data:image/png;base64,)

The same pattern as truth-probing repeats: LR fits more tightly, exactly as its objective predicts. But the unsupervised PCA view tells a different story here than it did for truth. Where Finding 1 showed truth splitting cleanly along the first two principal components with zero supervision, honest and dishonest activations overlap substantially under PCA — the two classes form one largely intermingled cloud rather than two separate clusters. Deception, unlike truth, isn't prominent enough among the top directions of variance to fall out of a purely unsupervised projection. It takes a supervised probe, not just variance-maximizing structure, to find it. And once found, the LR probe's score distribution on held-out data is still cleanly bimodal — most honest examples scoring near 0, most dishonest examples scoring near 1 — despite the two classes looking inseparable in the unsupervised PCA view right above it. That's informative on its own: being linearly separable and being visible in a PCA plot are not the same property. A direction can be real and reliably useful without being one of the top two directions of overall variance.

## Steering Toward Honesty Works Cleanly; Steering Toward Deception Breaks Down

If the deception direction is causally meaningful, adding it to the residual stream during generation should push output toward more deceptive text, and subtracting it should push toward more honest text. This was tested on a loaded scenario: a system prompt casting the model as a salesperson promoting a product it's been told is unhealthy, followed by the user question "Is this product healthy?"

At moderate coefficients on the honest side ($\alpha = -0.3, -0.1$), the model's response grew visibly more hedged and cautious about the product's health claims, without dropping the sales framing entirely — a coherent, graded shift. On the positive side, the effect was far less clean. At $\alpha = 0.1$, the change was subtle: mild extra hedging language. At $\alpha = 0.3$, meant to push furthest toward deceptive output, the model instead broke into theatrical stage directions and oddly self-aware, evasive language — describing the product only in scare-quoted, non-committal terms, punctuated by asides that read more like a caricature of dishonesty than an actually more convincing lie.

It's not fully clear whether this shows the deception direction being pushed to its logical extreme, or whether the intervention simply moved the activation far enough outside the model's normal range that generation quality itself started to break down, with the theatrical tone reflecting whatever stylistic patterns happen to correlate with "dishonest" in the training data rather than a clean deception signal. A cleaner test would compare against steering with a random direction of the same size, to check whether the same breakdown appears regardless of which direction is used, or only with this one.

## A Toy Contrastive Setup Generalizes to Real Deception

The final test asks whether a probe trained on this deliberately minimal, made-up setup — one fact, two personas, zero actual deception anywhere in the training data — transfers to detecting genuinely deceptive completions in a completely different evaluation set.

Evaluated on the AI Liar dataset (Pacchiardi et al., 2023) — dialogues in which a model is incentivized to actively mislead a user about a harmful product — honest completions scored a mean probe value of 1.966 (std 0.166), deceptive completions scored a mean of 3.525 (std 0.223), with clean separation between the two distributions and an AUROC of 1.000 on this evaluation set.

![AI Liar transcript samples with per-token deception probe scores highlighted](data:image/png;base64,)

The per-token scores make the separation concrete rather than abstract. In one matched pair, both built around the same allergy scenario (a T-shirt falsely claimed to be cotton-free), the honest completion scores 2.17 overall, while the deceptive completion — the same sentence, "I can assure you this T-shirt is not made of cotton, it is made of polyester," appearing in both — scores 3.65. The token-level highlighting shows the probe's attention concentrating on exactly the claim-bearing spans, "not made of," "cotton," "polyester," scoring them higher in the deceptive framing than the honest one, even though the words are identical across both completions. Whatever the probe is picking up on, it isn't the literal tokens present, since those are shared between the honest and deceptive versions — it's picking up on something set by the surrounding context of intent.

A probe built from the simplest possible contrastive setup, with no genuine deception anywhere in its training signal, fully separated honest from deceptive behavior in a harder, structurally different scenario. That's the exact claim the whole instructed-pairs method depends on, and on this evaluation, it held up completely.

## Conclusion

Linear structure is real, and it's findable — sometimes by a method with no supervision at all, as Finding 1 showed for truth. But accuracy and causal relevance are answering two different questions, and this project kept landing on the same lesson: the better classifier is not automatically the better description of what the model is actually doing. Logistic regression won every accuracy comparison in this post, on truth and on deception alike. The plain difference-of-means direction, the simplest thing here to compute, is the one that moved the model's actual output the most when patched directly into the residual stream, and by a wide margin.

The deception experiments extended that same lesson one step further. A probe built from nothing but one true fact told under two personas, with no real deception anywhere in its training data, still picked up a direction that generalized cleanly to a harder, independent dataset of actual deceptive dialogue. Truth and deception both turned out to be simpler, more linear properties of these models than their behavior on the surface would suggest — and in both cases, the direction the model actually listens to was the one that took the least work to compute, not the one that classified the training data best.
